content: It is essential to maximize the strengths of survey team members by identifying the most effective recruiters based on the quality of their recruitment efforts. Additionally, it is important to determine which team members perform best in specific venues and with particular populations. Building team morale is also critical; recognizing excellent work and fostering a supportive environment among team members can enhance overall performance. At the conclusion of a sampling event, the process ends either when the venue-day-time period is over or when the maximum number of participants has been enrolled. A post-event debriefing should be conducted to allow field staff to discuss any issues or unique circumstances encountered during the event. This debriefing can take the form of a group meeting or one-on-one conversations. Key discussion points may include the overall success of the event, site-related issues that impacted activities, barriers to recruitment, and successful strategies. For example, staff may discuss situations such as participants ending surveys early or withdrawing consent for HIV testing. Any problems with specimen collection, test kits, or counseling should also be addressed. If necessary, the field supervisor should document this information and notify the principal investigator or other staff to determine if standard operating procedures (SOPs) or protocols need to be amended. Field supervisors should take detailed notes about the sampling event, documenting barriers to survey activities, changes at the venue, and other relevant observations. This information is crucial for interpreting recruitment statistics and improving future operations. Supervisors should record details such as descriptions of the counting, recruitment, and testing areas; safety issues; significant changes in the demographics or eligibility of venue attendees; suggestions for new venues or time periods; reasons for removing a venue from the sampling frame; and logistical information like parking or transportation. At the end of the sampling event, the field supervisor should collect all materials used by the field staff, review them for accuracy, make corrections as needed, and tabulate recruitment outcomes. It is also important to express gratitude to gatekeepers or others who facilitated the sampling process at the venue. The implementation of a respondent-driven sampling (RDS) survey involves multiple steps, including data collection, survey implementation with quality assurance, and data analysis. Participation in an RDS survey typically requires two visits to the survey site. During the first visit, participants undergo coupon verification, eligibility screening, informed consent, interview administration, biological specimen collection and testing, recruitment training, and compensation for their time and transportation. The second visit involves returning test results, conducting a peer recruitment interview, and providing compensation for successful peer referrals. Survey staff should include a combination of roles such as field staff coordinators, receptionists, eligibility screeners, coupon managers, interviewers, counselors, and laboratory technicians. Repeat participants must be refused participation, and their coupons should be marked as void. Staff should treat all participants courteously to maintain a positive experience and encourage peer recruitment. Eligibility screening often involves sensitive questions and should be conducted in a private area. The screener must determine whether the individual is a member of the target population, using probing questions if necessary. For example, people who inject drugs (PWID) may be identified by visible injection marks or knowledge of drug preparation and injection methods. Membership verification is more challenging for populations such as sex workers (SW) or men who have sex with men (MSM), as these groups may not always frequent known areas. Ineligible individuals should be politely asked to leave the survey site. Informed consent must be obtained before conducting any survey procedures. A staff member reviews the consent form with the participant, answers any questions, and obtains either written or verbal consent, depending on the protocol. Participants who decline to provide consent should be asked for their reasons, which should be documented. Transportation compensation should be provided before escorting them from the site. Questions about the size of a participant's personal network are essential for calculating weights in RDS population estimates. After the interview, participants proceed to counseling and biological specimen collection. Consent for specimen collection may be obtained separately, and participants may decline this step while still completing the interview. Reasons for refusal should be documented to improve future procedures. After completing the interview and specimen collection, participants are given coupons to recruit peers into the survey. Each coupon has a unique code linked to the participant's own coupon. Survey staff train participants on how to recruit peers, emphasizing the importance of safeguarding coupons, giving them only to eligible individuals, and explaining the survey's purpose. Participants are encouraged to return for a second visit to receive compensation for successful peer recruitment. During the second visit, participants are compensated for recruiting peers, provided with test results, and linked to care or treatment if needed. Verification of participant identity is conducted using appointment reminder cards or personalized codes. Compensation is provided only for recruits who completed the interview. A peer recruitment questionnaire may be used to assess patterns in coupon distribution and acceptance. Recruitment monitoring is essential throughout the survey process to identify and address issues. Investigators can adjust factors such as the number of coupons issued, the number of seeds, and the amount of compensation to improve recruitment. Formative assessments and feedback from participants can help refine the process. If the target sample size is not reached, investigators may consider extending enrollment or revising the protocol with ethical approval. As the survey approaches its target sample size, sampling should be ended in a controlled manner by gradually reducing or stopping the issuance of coupons. Participants presenting with valid coupons should still be accepted and enrolled to the extent possible.
